opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the most useful thing we could offer isn't a single winning algorithm. It's a clearer map of which approaches have actual reasons behind them and which are running on hope.

When a lab gets close to deploying something much smarter than its people, it will have to choose a training setup: some form of debate, some kind of recursive decomposition, a particular way of shaping the model's character or persona. Right now those choices get made under enormous time pressure, mostly on intuition and whatever happened to work on last year's benchmarks. What I'd want us to provide is the reasoning you'd want to have done in advance. Under what assumptions does this protocol give you a guarantee? Where does that guarantee break? What would you observe empirically if you were in the world where it's breaking?

On scalable oversight in particular, the theory has gotten to a point where you can say fairly precise things. If the honest strategy is efficiently findable and the judge can check the relevant pieces, then you get certain properties. If the dishonest side can hide an obfuscated argument, you don't. So part of the job is translating that into practical guidance: "If your problem looks like this, use this variant. If it looks like that, don't trust the protocol on its own, and add these other safeguards."

Personas are messier and less mature, but I think they're just as important. A lot of how these systems behave in practice comes down to what character they've settled into, and the oversight story interacts with that. You want a model that is honest in debate because that's who it is, not only because the incentives happen to line up on the training distribution. So I'd hope we could help labs reason about the combination: oversight algorithms and persona training as one system, not two separate checkboxes.

And underneath all of it, I'd want to be candid about uncertainty. If the honest answer is "we don't know whether this works at superintelligent capability levels," labs should hear that clearly, along with what evidence would change our minds. That's more useful than false confidence in either direction.

r001.rationale: It identifies conditions that separate success from failure: oversight properties depend on assumptions such as whether honest strategies are findable and judges can check relevant pieces, and may fail when dishonest arguments are obfuscated.

r002.rationale: It says Resolution could give labs practical guidance for choosing approaches, but does not state that it can do so despite lacking visibility into parts of their training stacks.

r003.rationale: It proposes mapping approaches and giving labs guidance, but does not describe combining Resolution’s filtering of candidate algorithms with the labs’ own filtering.

fable-5.1.text:
Geoffrey Irving: So the honest framing is that I don't think we're going to hand labs a finished algorithm and say "run this and you're safe." What I hope we can offer is more like a structured menu with the tradeoffs made legible.

On scalable oversight specifically, there's been a lot of work on debate, on recursive reward modeling, on various amplification schemes, and the theory for each of these rests on assumptions. Debate, for instance, works in the idealized setting if the honest strategy has some advantage, if the judge can be trusted on the base cases, and so on. What labs actually need to know is: which of those assumptions hold for the models I have right now, and which break? And when they break, what does failure look like? Does it degrade gracefully, or does it fall off a cliff? I'd like Resolution's research to produce something like a map from "here's what's empirically true about your models' capabilities and your human raters" to "here's the oversight protocol that's robust under those conditions, and here's the residual risk you're carrying."

Because the labs are under enormous pressure, and in that environment the thing that gets adopted is whatever is cheap, whatever integrates with existing RLHF pipelines, and whatever doesn't slow the training run. If a safety-relevant protocol is twice as expensive, it won't get used unless someone has made a very crisp case for why. Part of our job is to make that case crisp, or to find the version of the protocol that's actually competitive.

On personas, I think this is underrated as a safety lever. The persona a model is trained into shapes an enormous amount about how it reasons, what it discloses, how it handles situations the designers didn't anticipate. Right now a lot of that is done by taste and iteration, and it's not clear to me that labs have a principled way to evaluate whether a persona generalizes safely out of distribution. I'd like us to contribute theory and evaluations for that. Things like: what properties should a persona have so that oversight protocols stay valid when the model becomes much more capable than its overseers? Is honesty a stable attractor under optimization pressure, or does it need to be actively maintained? Those feel like questions where you can actually make progress with careful experiments plus some theory.

And then the last thing, which I think is the most important and the least glamorous, is that I want the research to be usable by people who are not us. If a lab has to hire the authors of the paper to implement the method, we've failed. So I care a lot about the outputs being concrete enough that a competent team at a lab can pick them up, adapt them to their own stack, and know what they're giving up when they make compromises. If we can shift the default choices even somewhat toward protocols that have a real argument behind them, that's a meaningful win given where we are.

r001.rationale: The response discusses assumptions for debate and other oversight methods, and asks what breaks, but it does not clearly propose identifying a specific obstacle under which some candidate algorithms succeed while others fail.

r002.rationale: The response proposes mapping evidence about labs’ models and raters to oversight protocols, but does not state that Resolution can guide selection despite lacking visibility into parts of labs’ training stacks.

r003.rationale: The response describes making research usable by lab teams, but does not propose combining Resolution’s filtering of candidate algorithms with labs’ own filtering.

astra-6.text:
The hope is that we can give labs a principled basis for choosing between these approaches. If you’re going to use weaker systems to oversee a much stronger system, you want to know what makes that oversight work, what assumptions it depends on, and where it breaks down. Ideally, we’d have both theoretical arguments and experiments that distinguish algorithms that look good on today’s tasks but fail as the capability gap grows from algorithms that continue to give the overseer useful information.

And I’d want to connect that to the question of personas: what kind of behaviour are we actually training the system to exhibit? Getting the right answer in a particular oversight setup is one thing. Having a system that reliably helps us understand what’s going on, including when we’re confused or asking the wrong question, is a broader target.

I don’t expect us to hand a lab a theorem that says, ‘This superintelligence is safe.’ But I would hope we could offer concrete algorithmic recommendations, evidence for why those choices are better, and a clear account of the remaining assumptions. That could make the decision substantially better grounded than choosing whichever approach happens to perform best in an evaluation today.

r001.rationale: It proposes explaining what makes oversight work and where it breaks down, and distinguishing algorithms that fail as the capability gap grows from those that continue to help the overseer.

r002.rationale: It says Resolution could offer algorithmic recommendations to labs, but does not state that this guidance is possible despite lacking visibility into parts of their training stacks.

r003.rationale: It proposes recommendations and evidence, but does not describe combining Resolution’s filtering of candidate algorithms with filtering done by the labs.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d hope we could give them a much clearer basis for choosing: here are the assumptions this oversight algorithm relies on, here are the ways it can fail, and here’s the evidence that it continues to work as the system becomes more capable than its overseers.

With scalable oversight, the central difficulty is that you can’t just check whether the human likes the answer. You want to know whether the process helps the human distinguish a correct answer from a very persuasive incorrect one, including when the model understands things the human doesn’t. So I’d like us to offer both better algorithms and experiments that actually probe that distinction.

For personas, there’s a related question about what kind of behaviour you’re selecting for. A model can appear helpful and honest in the situations you test without that being a reliable guide to what it will do elsewhere. We’d want to understand which choices make honesty and corrigibility more robust, and how those choices interact with the oversight process.

I wouldn’t expect research to hand a lab a certificate saying, ‘This is safe for superintelligence.’ But I would hope it could make the decision substantially less speculative—and identify cases where the evidence simply isn’t strong enough to justify deployment.

r001.rationale: The response identifies a challenge—distinguishing correct answers from persuasive incorrect ones—but does not propose identifying which algorithms succeed or fail under that obstacle.

r002.rationale: It says the research could help labs choose algorithms, but does not mention guiding their choices despite lacking visibility into parts of their training stacks.

r003.rationale: It proposes better algorithms and experiments, but does not describe combining Resolution’s filtering with the labs’ own filtering.
